name: Manage truckload drivers' hours and home time
summary: Each week a driver manager keeps every company truckload driver legal, loaded and on track to get home on the promised day. The manager reads hours left from the electronic logs, tells load planners when and where each truck frees up, checks that planned trips fit the daily and cycle limits, and makes check calls during the week. Pay questions go to the driver pay clerk, out-of-rotation time off to the operations manager, and drivers who look likely to quit to a stay conversation and, if they leave, to recruiting. The work is slow and error-prone because it runs on phone calls and in-cab messages, because a late unload or a storm can wreck a home-time plan, and because before the June 2021 ELD mandate many domestic drivers still used paper logs.

baseline.org_archetype: A Canadian LTL and truckload carrier of about 3,000 employees whose truckload division runs about 430 company drivers and 380 owner-operators across Canada and into the US.
baseline.notes: One case is one company driver's week. Owner-operators are dispatched by the same driver managers but are outside this process's volume, which follows the organisation file.

trigger: A new week starts for an active company truckload driver, with hours-of-service records carried from the trips of the week before, or a newly hired driver joins a driver manager's board.
end_state: The week is closed with the driver's availability and home time recorded, or the driver resigns and a vacancy is raised with recruiting.

volume.seasonality: Flat across the year because the driver count changes slowly; fewer active drivers in spring 2020 when COVID-19 cut volumes, and more hours problems in the autumn peak and in winter storms.

evidence.note: About 430 company truckload drivers in the organisation file times 4.33 weeks a month is about 1,860 driver-weeks; the range allows for vacancies.

Touch time of about 64 minutes per driver-week times 1,850 driver-weeks gives about 15 FTE; the organisation file's 36 driver managers also dispatch owner-operators and handle trip problems in other processes.
Driver time on home-time requests only; stands for all 430 company drivers (300 long-haul and 130 regional). Driving time is counted in trip execution.
Rerouting drivers toward home on about 35% of driver-weeks; author's estimate.
Time-off approvals and stay conversations; author's estimate.

roles.title: Driver pay and owner-operator settlements clerk

evidence.note: Driver pay questions on about 18% of driver-weeks; the clerk role covers driver pay as well as owner-operator settlements.

roles.title: Compliance specialist (hours of service and driver files)

evidence.note: Recording violations and remedial action as SOR/2005-313 s. 87 requires; time is the author's estimate.
Night and weekend driver calls on about 15% of driver-weeks; author's estimate.
Requisitions for about 19 truckload driver resignations a month; author's estimate.

systems.name: Electronic logging devices and telematics platform
Transportation management system (LTL and truckload operations, billing, rating)
Email, phone system and contact centre software
Safety management system (driver files, collisions, roadside inspections)

steps.name: Open the weekly hours and home-time board
steps.description: On Monday morning the driver manager opens the ELD portal and the TMS driver board for the driver, reads the hours left in the current cycle, the date of the last 36-hour reset and the home-time date promised to the driver. Before mid-2021 many domestic drivers still sent paper logs, so the manager also reads the last log sheets faxed or scanned in.

evidence.note: Hours limits from SOR/2005-313; ELD mandate from June 2021 with progressive enforcement to June 2022. Driver manager practice at Canadian truckload carriers 2019-2022 from general knowledge; times are the author's estimate per driver-week.

steps.name: Update projected time available in the TMS
steps.description: The driver manager types the driver's projected time and place of availability and the home-by date into the TMS so load planners see when and where the truck frees up. The manager adds notes on preferred lanes, border-crossing documents and any restrictions such as no Quebec loads or no reefer.

error.defect_description: Wrong projected time or place of availability, so a load is planned that the driver cannot reach in time.

evidence.note: Driver manager practice at Canadian truckload carriers 2019-2022 from general knowledge; times are the author's estimate per driver-week.

steps.name: Driver confirms home-time request
steps.description: The driver answers the manager's ELD or phone message at the next stop, confirming the day he or she wants to be home, any appointments, and whether he or she will take a full reset at home. Long-haul drivers usually ask for two to four days at home after ten to fourteen days out.

next.condition: home time falls this week and the next loads must head toward home

evidence.note: Long-haul home-time pattern and response times are the author's estimate from general industry knowledge.

steps.name: Negotiate loads that route the driver home
steps.description: The driver manager calls the load planner with the home-by date and the planner searches open loads in the TMS for one delivering near the driver's home terminal. If none fits, they agree to swap loads between drivers or to deadhead the truck home empty, which costs empty miles.

error.defect_description: Planner books a load whose delivery appointment leaves no room for the home date.

evidence.note: Load-planner and driver-manager negotiation is common practice at truckload fleets; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Check the planned trip against hours available
steps.description: The driver manager compares the pickup and delivery appointments of the planned loads with the hours shown in the ELD: 13 hours of driving and 14 on duty in a day, no driving after 16 hours elapsed, and 70 hours in 7 days. If the trip cannot be run legally, the manager asks the planner to swap the load.

error.defect_description: A trip that cannot be completed within hours is approved.

control.basis: Commercial Vehicle Drivers Hours of Service Regulations SOR/2005-313, s. 87 (carrier must monitor each driver's compliance) and ss. 12-14, 26-28 (daily and cycle limits); US 49 CFR Part 395 on cross-border trips

next.condition: trip fits hours and home time
trip does not fit; load swapped

evidence.note: Limits from SOR/2005-313; the driver-manager duty to coach on driving time and HOS compliance from the job posting. Share of swaps is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Send load details and trip plan to the driver
steps.description: The driver manager sends the load numbers, pickup and delivery appointments, routing notes and fuel stops to the driver's in-cab unit and confirms the driver has accepted. The manager answers questions on directions, border documents and customer rules.

evidence.note: Giving drivers complete load information and routing is listed in the driver-manager posting; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: ELD flags hours and trip exceptions
steps.description: While the driver runs, the ELD and telematics platform tracks duty status and raises alerts when the driver nears the daily or cycle limit, misses a 30-minute US break, or records unassigned driving. Before mid-2021 paper-log drivers produced no live alerts, so problems surfaced only when the logs were audited.

next.condition: hours shortfall or alert needs action

evidence.note: ELD mandate and phase-in from Today's Trucking; share of weeks with an hours problem is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Coach the driver and replan around the hours limit
steps.description: The driver manager calls the driver, works out where the driver can legally stop, and either moves the delivery appointment, plans a 36-hour reset, or asks the planner to repower the load with another driver. The manager records the remedial action against the driver.

control.basis: Commercial Vehicle Drivers Hours of Service Regulations SOR/2005-313, s. 87 (carrier must monitor each driver's compliance) and ss. 12-14, 26-28 (daily and cycle limits); US 49 CFR Part 395 on cross-border trips

next.condition: a violation occurred and must be recorded

evidence.note: Remedial action and its recording are required by SOR/2005-313 s. 87(2); share and times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Record the violation and remedial action
steps.description: The compliance specialist reviews the log, enters the violation, its date and the remedial action in the safety system, and sends a written warning or coaching referral according to the progressive discipline policy. Repeat offenders go to the safety manager.

control.basis: SOR/2005-313 s. 87(2): record dates of non-compliance and the remedial action taken

evidence.note: Record-keeping duty from SOR/2005-313 s. 87(2); handling times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Mid-week check call with the driver
steps.description: The driver manager calls or messages the driver to ask how the trip is going, check fuel and equipment problems, and confirm the home-time date still holds. Drivers raise pay questions, family matters and complaints about waiting times here.

next.condition: night or weekend call goes to the after-hours desk

evidence.note: Addressing driver concerns and monitoring ETAs are driver-manager duties in the posting; branch shares are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Look up trip pay and answer the pay question
steps.description: The driver pay clerk opens the driver's pay record in the TMS and payroll system, compares paid miles with the practical route miles, and checks whether stop pay, layover or border pay was entered. The clerk writes the answer or keys a correction for the next pay run.

error.defect_description: Wrong miles or missing accessorial pay confirmed as correct.

evidence.note: Pay questions are a frequent driver complaint; share and handling time are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Relay the pay answer to the driver
steps.description: The driver manager passes the clerk's answer to the driver and, where pay was short, tells the driver when the correction will appear. Unresolved pay complaints are noted on the driver's file because they raise the risk of the driver leaving.

evidence.note: Driver manager practice at Canadian truckload carriers 2019-2022 from general knowledge; times are the author's estimate per driver-week.

steps.name: Assess a personal issue or time-off request
steps.description: The driver manager listens to the driver's request, such as a sick family member, a medical appointment or a request for extra days, checks the driver's rotation and the loads already planned, and decides whether to ask for an early trip home.

evidence.note: Processing time-off requests is listed in the posting; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Approve time off or an emergency trip home
steps.description: The truckload operations manager approves time off outside the rotation or an empty move to bring the driver home, weighing the cost of deadhead miles and the uncovered loads against retention. Approved requests go back to the planner.

control.basis: Company home-time and leave policy: manager approval for time off outside the rotation

next.condition: time off fits the existing plan

evidence.note: Approval of out-of-rotation time off by the operations manager is the author's assumption of common policy.

steps.name: After-hours dispatcher handles a night or weekend call
steps.description: The after-hours dispatcher takes the driver's call outside office hours, for example a late unload, a refused load or a breakdown, updates the TMS notes and, if hours or home time are affected, leaves a note for the driver manager for the next morning.

evidence.note: After-hours desks are common at truckload fleets; share and times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Check whether home time falls this week
steps.description: The driver manager checks the trip plan against the home-by date to see whether the driver will reach home before the week ends. Drivers who stay out continue on loads; drivers going home are watched on the last leg.

evidence.note: Share of driver-weeks with home time mixes long-haul drivers home every second week and regional drivers home weekly; author's estimate.

steps.name: Driver runs the last leg home
steps.description: The driver delivers the last load and drives the tractor to the home terminal or, where policy allows, to a parking spot near home. The time is ordinary driving already paid as trip miles, so no extra labour is counted here.

next.condition: late unload, storm or road closure delays the driver

evidence.note: Last-leg timing and the share of missed home dates are the author's estimate; missed home time is a common driver complaint.

steps.name: Replan after a delay pushes back home time
steps.description: When a winter storm, a highway closure or a long wait at a customer delays the driver, the driver manager rebooks the delivery, tells the driver the new home date and apologises. The manager notes the missed home time because repeated misses predict resignations.

evidence.note: Winter weather and customer delays are common causes of missed home time in Canada; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Confirm the driver is back on duty after home time
steps.description: After the driver's days at home, the driver manager checks in the ELD that the driver has taken the reset and is back on duty, and confirms the tractor is ready for the next dispatch. The tractor sits parked while the driver is home.

evidence.note: A cycle reset needs at least 36 consecutive hours off duty (s. 28); home stays of 36 to 72 hours are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Second check call for drivers staying out
steps.description: For drivers not going home this week, the driver manager makes a second call late in the week to confirm the next home date, ask about rest and fatigue and check that the weekend loads still fit the hours left in the cycle.

evidence.note: Driver manager practice at Canadian truckload carriers 2019-2022 from general knowledge; times are the author's estimate per driver-week.

steps.name: Review the driver's week against targets
steps.description: At the end of the week the driver manager reviews the driver's paid miles, revenue, idle time, home time delivered against promised and any complaints, using the weekly BI report. Low miles, missed home time and pay disputes mark a driver as a retention risk.

evidence.note: Weekly miles review and retention flags are common practice; author's estimate.

steps.name: Hold a stay conversation with an at-risk driver
steps.description: The truckload operations manager calls the driver to hear the complaint and may offer a different lane, a regional run, a newer tractor or a fixed home-time pattern. The outcome is recorded on the driver's file.

evidence.note: Turnover context: 90% at large US truckload fleets in 2020. The resignation rate is set so about 1% of driver-weeks end in a resignation, about 55% a year, close to the organisation file's 50% assumption.

steps.name: Close out the departing driver and notify recruiting
steps.description: The driver manager arranges the driver's last trip to the terminal, collects the fuel card and tractor keys, and emails recruiting and payroll with the leaving date and the seat to be filled.

evidence.note: Driver manager practice at Canadian truckload carriers 2019-2022 from general knowledge; times are the author's estimate per driver-week.

steps.name: Open a requisition for a replacement driver
steps.description: The driver recruiter logs the vacancy in the applicant tracking system with the domicile, lane type and start date, and adds it to the week's job advertisements.

evidence.note: Recruiting intake time is the author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Hours shortfall needs a replan
exceptions.description: The ELD shows the driver cannot legally finish the planned trip, so the manager moves the appointment, plans a reset or repowers the load.

exceptions.name: Hours violation recorded
exceptions.description: A violation occurs and the compliance specialist records it with the remedial action.

exceptions.name: Missed home time
exceptions.description: A storm, road closure or late unload delays the driver's arrival home and the manager rebooks the home date.

exceptions.name: Pay question
exceptions.description: The driver disputes miles or missing accessorial pay and the pay clerk investigates.

exceptions.name: Resignation
exceptions.description: An at-risk driver resigns after a stay conversation and recruiting opens a requisition.

evidence.note: The unit of work is a calendar week, so the cycle is about seven days by definition; a week with a missed home date runs a little longer.

benchmarks.population: US truckload fleets over USD 30 million revenue, 2020

evidence.note: US figure; the organisation file assumes about 50% for this Canadian carrier.

benchmarks.population: Commercial vehicle drivers in Canada south of latitude 60

evidence.note: SOR/2005-313 s. 12(1); 14 h on duty, 16 h elapsed, 70 h in 7 days on cycle 1.
Common span quoted in the industry and in the organisation file's description of 30 to 45 drivers; no source opened gives a figure.

pain_points.description: Missed home time after storms, road closures and long waits at customers is a main reason truckload drivers quit.

evidence.note: Turnover level from ATA; the link to home time is the author's general knowledge.

pain_points.description: Before the June 2021 ELD mandate, paper-log drivers gave no live hours data, so managers planned trips on drivers' word and found violations only at the log audit.

evidence.note: Mandate date and phase-in from Today's Trucking.

pain_points.description: Pay questions bounce between driver, driver manager and pay clerk, and each unresolved one adds to the risk of resignation.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of truckload operations.

pain_points.description: Routing a driver home competes with covering customer loads, so planners and driver managers negotiate by phone each week.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

sources.title: Commercial Vehicle Drivers Hours of Service Regulations (SOR/2005-313)
sources.publisher: Government of Canada, Justice Laws Website
sources.supports: South of 60 degrees: 13 h driving and 14 h on duty per day (s. 12), no driving after 16 h elapsed (s. 13(3)), 10 h off duty per day (s. 14); cycle 1 of 70 h in 7 days (s. 26), cycle 2 of 120 h in 14 days (s. 27); cycle reset after 36 h (cycle 1) or 72 h (cycle 2) off duty (s. 28); the motor carrier must monitor each driver's compliance and record remedial action (s. 87).

sources.title: Enforcement of Canada's ELD mandate to be phased in over a year
sources.supports: Transport Canada kept the 12 June 2021 ELD mandate date with a 12-month progressive enforcement period of education and awareness; full enforcement expected from June 2022.

sources.title: Turnover Remained Unchanged at Large Truckload Fleets in Fourth Quarter
sources.supports: Annualised driver turnover in 2020: large truckload fleets 90% (92% in Q4), small truckload 69%, LTL 13%; tight driver market.

sources.title: Driver Manager, Day & Ross (Duncan, OK) job posting
sources.supports: Driver manager duties at a Canadian-owned carrier: give drivers complete load information, coach on departure and driving time for on-time delivery and hours-of-service compliance, coach on the ELD, monitor ELD messages and TMS trip flow, process time-off requests, support driver retention; day shifts from 5 AM. A later posting used as a description of a long-standing role.

assumptions: The unit of work is one company driver's week, following the organisation file (430 company drivers, about 1,850 driver-weeks a month). Owner-operators are handled by the same driver managers but are not counted here; if they were, the volume would be about 3,500 driver-weeks a month.
The driver step uses the long-haul driver role to stand for both long-haul and regional company drivers; regional drivers go home weekly, which is folded into the 55% share of weeks with home time.
Times and branch shares are tier C estimates: no public source opened gives driver-manager task times. The hours rules come from SOR/2005-313 and the duties from a driver-manager job posting.
Waits are calendar time across a week; the home-time path and the stay-out path are both set to take about seven days, so the simulated cycle time reflects the weekly unit rather than queue delays.
The resignation branch is tuned so that about 1% of driver-weeks end in a resignation (about 55% annual turnover), close to the organisation file's assumption of 50%.
The company tractor is listed without a running cost because it sits parked, not running, while the driver is home; the step records how long it is out of service.
Loaded costs come from the organisation file (x1.30 for hourly field staff, x1.35 for salaried office staff).

Staffing: the steps imply about 15 FTE of driver-manager time for 430 drivers, about 29 drivers per FTE. The organisation file's 36 driver managers at 30 to 45 drivers each would cover 1,080 to 1,620 drivers, more than the 810 company and owner-operator drivers; the remaining driver-manager time is assumed to go to owner-operators and trip problems in other processes.
